facts.text: On this date in 1789, the U.S. Congress passed the Judiciary Act, creating the Supreme Court — a body the Constitution had authorized but left almost entirely undefined.
On this date in 1946, the Cannes Film Festival held its very first edition, delayed six years by World War II from its originally scheduled 1939 debut.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, packing over 111,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any borough of New York, any arrondissement of Paris.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding roughly 60% of the world's fresh surface lake water within its borders.
The country with the highest median age is not Japan — it is Monaco, where the median resident is over 55 years old, a product of wealth, longevity, and almost no youth immigration.

On this day in 1869, Black Friday struck Wall Street. Jay Gould and James Fisk had cornered the gold market; when Grant ordered the Treasury to sell, gold collapsed 20% in minutes and ruined thousands of traders.

On this day in 1998, the Federal Reserve orchestrated a $3.6B bailout of Long-Term Capital Management — a hedge fund run by two Nobel laureates whose models simply hadn't accounted for Russia defaulting.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792 by 24 brokers who agreed not to trade with outsiders. The entire founding document is 68 words long.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6B — the largest in history — yet it listed on only the Riyadh exchange. The company was considered too large for any single foreign market to absorb cleanly.

The Dutch East India Company, often called the first modern corporation, was at its peak worth an estimated $8 trillion in today's dollars — more than the current combined value of Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia.

On this date in 1970, Luna 16 became the first uncrewed spacecraft to land on the Moon and return samples to Earth — Soviet engineers had built a robot geologist that worked perfectly without a single human on board.
On this date in 2014, India's Mars Orbiter Mission entered Martian orbit, making India the first nation to succeed on its very first attempt — a feat neither the US nor Soviet Union managed.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere roughly the size of a city, meaning a single teaspoon of its matter would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces virtually all its atoms roughly every seven years, yet the pattern that makes you *you* persists — identity is not matter but information encoded in matter.

The mantis shrimp sees with 16 types of color receptors compared to the human eye's 3, yet research shows it processes color *worse* than humans — more channels, paradoxically, means less discrimination.
On this day in 1789, Congress established the U.S. federal judiciary — the same week it passed the Bill of Rights. The Supreme Court didn't hold its first session for another four months.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Medieval students were cramming for exams before Tenochtitlan existed.

On this day in 1957, federal troops escorted nine Black students into a Little Rock school while Eisenhower watched from the White House — 89 years after the 14th Amendment had promised equal protection.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was separated from Khufu by 2,500 years; from Armstrong by only 2,000.
Nintendo was founded in 1889, selling playing cards. The company that made Game Boy predates commercial electricity in most of the world.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in 2012, it spread so fast it now appears in several translation dictionaries.

Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word meaning the shared, wordless look between two people who both want something but neither will initiate. Linguists consider it one of the most concise expressions of human awkwardness ever recorded.

On this day in 1789, the U.S. Congress proposed the Bill of Rights — and the word 'inalienable' nearly lost to 'unalienable'. Jefferson preferred the latter; both mean incapable of being taken away, from Latin 'alienare', to transfer ownership.

Hiraeth (Welsh, n.): a longing for a home that may never have existed, blending nostalgia, grief, and belonging into a single untranslatable ache. English has borrowed it wholesale because nothing else comes close.

Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of a used bookshop, coined by John Koenig in his Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows. It fuses 'vellum' with the archaic 'ichor', the fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting the network's energy consumption by roughly 99.95% overnight.
Bitcoin's genesis block contains the text 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — a timestamp, a political statement, and a proof that no coins were premined before Jan 3, 2009.
On this date in 2014, the U.S. Marshals auctioned 29,656 BTC seized from Silk Road to venture capitalist Tim Draper, who bid in bulk lots specifically to win the entire offering.
The smallest unit of bitcoin, one satoshi, is 0.00000001 BTC — at peak 2024 prices, a single satoshi briefly exceeded one U.S. cent in purchasing power.
Ethereum's EIP-1559, activated in August 2021, introduced a base fee that is permanently burned rather than paid to miners, removing over 1 million ETH from circulation within its first year.
On this date in 2022, DeepMind published AlphaTensor — the first AI to discover novel matrix multiplication algorithms, beating a 50-year-old human record for 4×4 matrices.
On this date in 2009, Google quietly filed a patent for a neural network ad-ranking system, seven years before deep learning became its core infrastructure.
GPT-4's training run consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average U.S. homes.
The original 1956 Dartmouth AI proposal requested funding for 10 researchers over 2 months, estimating that was sufficient to solve most of the field's core problems.
RLHF, the technique now central to aligning large language models, was first described in a 2017 OpenAI paper about teaching robots to backflip from human preference ratings.
